query: The First Supper The first supper is twelve courses in a town house with a ceiling painted with clouds. You're seated between a retired magistrate and a woman who owns half the orchards in the valley. Both of them have read about you. Both of them want to see whether you're as interesting as the Ledger said. The magistrate has an opinion on every course, and is plainly waiting for somebody to disagree with him. Argue with the magistrate You tell the magistrate he's wrong about the soup, and then about a famous old trial, and he's delighted: nobody has disagreed with him since he retired. By the ninth course the whole table is listening to the two of you. Someone at the far end asks your name twice, to remember it. You take the magistrate on over an old case, and turn out to have the facts backwards, in front of the man who heard it. The orchard woman changes the subject, kindly, which is worse. You spend the last three courses very interested in your soup. Ask about her orchards You leave the magistrate to the soup. You ask the orchard woman about her orchards, and she talks for an hour, delighted, about apple blight. The table thinks you're a little dull. She thinks you're the best guest she's had in years.
